headline: Ancient Knowledge Meets Modern Science to Protect Fish and Reefs
meta_description: Australian scientists and Bardi Jawi rangers reveal how traditional ecological knowledge confirms the vital connection between reef and mangrove ecosystems.
summary_short: A decade-long partnership between Western scientists and Indigenous rangers in Australia's Kimberley region has proven what Traditional Owners knew for millennia: fish s…
body:
For ten years, Bardi Jawi rangers and traditional owners in northwestern Australia have worked alongside scientists from the Australian Institute of Marine Science to study their mangrove and reef ecosystems. A 2026 study published in Ocean & Coastal Management revealed something remarkable: ten fish species culturally vital to Bardi Jawi fishing practices migrated between reefs and mangroves far more than other species, moving beyond their nursery stages and using both ecosystems as refuge. What struck many as a scientific breakthrough was, for the Bardi Jawi, simply confirmation. As Phillip McCarthy, coordinator of the Bardi Jawi men's ranger program, told researchers: "We knew most of it. But the science confirmed it. They told us, 'You were right.'"

The partnership revealed something equally important: the value of recognizing Indigenous peoples as scientists in their own right. Over thirty thousand years, Bardi Jawi knowledge has been refined through careful observation and experimentation—testing which areas sustained life, understanding tidal movements, tracking species behavior. This accumulated wisdom guided the design of both the Bardi Jawi Indigenous Protected Area and the Bardi Jawi Gaarra Marine Park, established to safeguard their traditional fishing grounds across 95,000 hectares of land and 204,000 hectares of ocean.

Yet the study also offered something new to the Bardi Jawi: understanding how climate change and environmental pressures might threaten either ecosystem, potentially leaving certain species unable to survive. The collaboration didn't diminish traditional knowledge—it deepened it. In recognizing Indigenous rangers and elders as co-authors in scientific journals, the research demonstrated that effective conservation happens not when one knowledge system replaces another, but when both are honored as essential to protecting the living world.
quick_facts: Bardi Jawi rangers and Australian marine scientists collaborated for a decade
Ten culturally important fish species migrate between reefs and mangroves
Study guided design of 204,000-hectare marine park in Kimberley region
Traditional knowledge accumulated over 30,000 years confirmed by modern science
Indigenous rangers listed as co-authors in Ocean & Coastal Management journal
